title: Law, regulation, proposal, ruling, contract or guidance

sources.claim: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 (January 26, 2023) and its Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1, July 26, 2024) are intended for voluntary use: guidance, not a law.

sections.skill: Tell a law, regulation, bill, ruling, contract and guidance apart

questions.prompt: Who passes a law (statute)?

choices.text: A company that makes AI tools, when it writes the terms that its users agree to

questions.intro: Rules about AI come in different forms with different force. A LAW (statute) is passed by a legislature, such as Congress or a state legislature. A REGULATION is a detailed rule made by a government agency under a law. A PROPOSED BILL is not law until it passes. A COURT RULING decides a case and can guide later cases, depending on the court. A CONTRACT, such as a tool's terms of service, binds the people who agree to it. VOLUNTARY GUIDANCE, such as the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (January 2023), offers advice but is not a law. This course gives general information, not legal advice.

sections.skill: Compare kinds of rules with rules at a school

questions.prompt: A required number of school days set by the state is like what?
questions.intro: At school, a state LAW might require a number of school days. The school district makes detailed REGULATIONS, like the bell schedule. A student council PROPOSAL is not a rule until adopted. A principal's DECISION settles one student's case. A sports team's signed AGREEMENT binds the players who signed it. A teacher's study TIPS are helpful advice, not rules. Each has different force.

sections.skill: Check the status and date of AI rules

questions.prompt: A news story says "New AI law!" but describes an agency's draft. What is it really?

choices.text: A final law that took effect the moment the agency posted the draft on its website
A draft that is not yet final

questions.correct_answer: A draft that is not yet final
questions.intro: News stories blur these forms. "New AI law!" may describe a bill that has not passed, an agency's draft, or one judge's ruling in a single case. Ask: Who made it? Has it taken effect, and when? Where does it apply? Is it binding, or advice? Rules also change: bills fail, regulations are revised, and higher courts can overturn rulings. Always check the date and current status before relying on a rule.
